prompt: Match each piece of the planner to the kind of state it is.

pairs.left: the half-typed minutes of a new session

prompt: The user swipes the planner away on purpose and opens it again. What should the half-typed session form show?

choices.text: The half-typed minutes, as after a kill
choices.why: UI state survives the system, not the user's choice to start again.

choices.text: An error saying the draft was lost
choices.why: Nothing was lost by accident; the user closed it.

choices.text: Nothing: they chose a fresh start
choices.why: Right. UI state is gone after the user closes the screen, and that is correct.

choices.text: The last session the user submitted
choices.why: That is data, and it belongs in the list, not in the form.

prompt: Why should the planner not save the week's total in its UI state?

choices.text: It is derived from the data, and a saved copy can go stale
choices.why: Right. Recompute it from the plan after a restore.

choices.text: Numbers cannot be saved in saved state
choices.why: Numbers can; the scroll position is one.

choices.text: It is too large to fit in the saved state
choices.why: It is three small numbers.

choices.text: Totals are private data, and saved state can be read by other apps on the phone
choices.why: Privacy is not the reason; staleness is.

prompt: The user had typed "4" on the way to "45" when the app was killed. What does the lesson say to save?

choices.text: Nothing, because "4" is not a valid session length yet
choices.why: Validity is for submitting, not for saving where the user was.

choices.text: A session of 4 minutes, added to the plan
choices.why: That turns a half-typed field into data the user never submitted.

choices.text: The default value of the field
choices.why: That throws the user's typing away.

choices.text: The raw string "4", as the user left it
choices.why: Right. The user expects to find exactly what they typed.

prompt: What does Android do by default when the user turns the phone?

choices.text: Kills the process and starts a new one
choices.why: The process stays alive; only the Activity is rebuilt.

choices.text: Destroys the Activity and creates a new one
choices.why: Right, with onDestroy and then onCreate in the new configuration.

choices.text: Nothing; only the views are resized
choices.why: That is closer to what iOS does.

choices.text: Suspends the app until the rotation ends
choices.why: Suspension is a background state, not part of a rotation.

prompt: A list loaded from the network is kept in a ViewModel. What happens to it after a rotation, and after the system kills the process?

choices.text: It survives both
choices.why: A ViewModel lives in the process, and the kill takes the process.

choices.text: It survives the rotation, not the kill
choices.why: Right. Android's guide says ViewModels are destroyed during a system-initiated process death.

choices.text: It survives the kill but not the rotation
choices.why: That is the opposite of what Android's table says.

choices.text: It survives neither
choices.why: Surviving a rotation is what a ViewModel is for.

prompt: Which of these survive the system killing the process, according to Android's table? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: saved state
choices.why: Yes: it is held by the system, outside the process.

choices.text: persistent storage
choices.why: Yes: it is on disk or the network.

choices.text: a ViewModel
choices.why: It is in memory, in the process that died.

choices.text: a field of the Activity
choices.why: It does not even survive a rotation.

prompt: An Android app keeps its form through a rotation using only a ViewModel. What has that proved about process death?

choices.text: That iOS will restore it too
choices.why: iOS has no ViewModel and no rotation rebuild.

choices.text: That the form survives a kill as well
choices.why: The ViewModel is in the process the kill takes.

choices.text: That the app will crash with TransactionTooLargeException
choices.why: A ViewModel does not go through the Binder buffer.

choices.text: Nothing about the save path, which a turn never exercises
choices.why: Right. The kill takes the ViewModel too, so it has to be tested on its own.

prompt: Why does a turned iPhone not lose the planner's form the way a turned Android phone can?

choices.text: It lays the views out again
choices.why: Right: nothing is destroyed, so only a kill is a danger there.

choices.text: iPhones cannot be rotated
choices.why: They can; the views are told their size changed.

choices.text: iOS saves every form automatically
choices.why: Nothing is saved; nothing is destroyed either.

choices.text: SwiftUI keeps every form in a ViewModel that survives the rotation
choices.why: ViewModel is Android's; the reason is that nothing is rebuilt.

prompt: Match each platform to how it keeps UI state across a kill.

pairs.right: the app writes it to storage itself

prompt: When does Android actually write the values given to saved state?

choices.text: The instant each value changes
choices.why: The guide says writes in between are deferred to the next stop.

choices.text: In onDestroy
choices.why: onDestroy may never run.

choices.text: When the Activity is stopped
choices.why: Right: on the way to the background, lesson 4's last reliable moment.

choices.text: Once a minute, on a system timer
choices.why: There is no such timer.

prompt: Which of these does Apple's page say about @SceneStorage?

choices.text: It should be lightweight, and not hold sensitive data
choices.why: Right, the same limits Android puts on saved state.

choices.text: It is saved the instant a value changes
choices.why: The page says the system makes no guarantees about when it is persisted.

choices.text: It is the right place for model data
choices.why: The page says model data should not be stored there.

choices.text: It is shared between all of an app's scenes
choices.why: Each scene has its own.

prompt: A React Native app saves its form to AsyncStorage on the way to the background. What does that storage do that platform saved state does not?

choices.text: Survives a rotation
choices.why: Saved state survives a rotation too.

choices.text: Survives a system kill
choices.why: Platform saved state does that as well.

choices.text: Survives the user closing the app on purpose
choices.why: Right, so the app has to clear it on submit and decide what is too old to offer.

choices.text: Gets restored by the system automatically
choices.why: The app reads it back itself; nothing is automatic.

prompt: node restore.ts use prints its screen, saves 80 bytes and is killed. Why does its exit handler never print goodbye?

choices.text: The handler was registered after the kill
choices.why: It was registered a few lines before.

choices.text: SIGKILL ends the process without running any more of its code
choices.why: Right: lesson 4's silent kill, from the inside.

choices.text: Node.js does not support exit handlers in .ts files
choices.why: It does; a normal exit would run it.

choices.text: The terminal cut the last line of output when the process ended
choices.why: Nothing was printed to cut.

prompt: The shell reports the killed process with an exit status of 128 plus the signal's number. SIGKILL is signal 9. What status does it print?
After the restore, the week's numbers appear on screen although they were not in saved-state.json. Where did they come from?

choices.text: From a cache that Node.js keeps on disk between one run and the next
choices.why: Each run is a new process with nothing from the old one.

choices.text: The file held them in a hidden field
choices.why: The file is shown whole: course id, scroll and draft.

choices.text: From the git repository
choices.why: git holds the program, not the numbers.

choices.text: They were computed again from the plan, which is data
choices.why: Right. Derived values are recomputed, not saved.

prompt: The saved state names the course as mobile, and the title comes from the data. What happens if the course is renamed while the app is dead?

choices.text: The old title comes back from the saved state
choices.why: The saved state holds no title.

choices.text: The restore fails because the id changed
choices.why: Renaming changes the title, not the id.

choices.text: The screen comes back with the new name
choices.why: Right. The id is looked up in the data as it is now.

choices.text: Both titles appear side by side
choices.why: There is only one title to show.

prompt: Put the round trip in order.
items: draw the screen from the UI state
write the UI state on the way to the background
the process is killed, with no callback
a new process reads the saved state

prompt: Android's guide recommends keeping saved state under how many kilobytes?
Saved with ids only, the planner's screen is 80 bytes. What happens to that size as the user adds thousands of sessions?

choices.text: It stays the same
choices.why: Right. The same id, scroll position and draft, however large the plan.

choices.text: It grows with every session
choices.why: That is the whole-plan version.

choices.text: It doubles every thousand sessions
choices.why: Nothing in it depends on the sessions.

choices.text: It shrinks, because old sessions are dropped
choices.why: Nothing is dropped; nothing is added.

prompt: On Android 7.0 and later, what happens when a transaction exceeds the Binder buffer?

choices.text: The system silently drops the extra bytes
choices.why: It is loud: an exception.

choices.text: A warning appears in the log, and the app carries on as if nothing happened
choices.why: That was the behaviour before Android 7.0.

choices.text: The saved state is written to disk instead
choices.why: Nothing moves it to disk on its own.

choices.text: A TransactionTooLargeException is thrown as a runtime exception
choices.why: Right, which ends the app unless something catches it.

prompt: A course is deleted on another device while the planner is dead, and the saved state still names it. What does the lesson prefer to an empty screen?

choices.text: Recreating the course from the saved id
choices.why: An id carries no course to recreate, and the user deleted it.

choices.text: Handling it on purpose: refuse loudly, or fall back to the list and say why
choices.why: Right. With ids, staleness is a lookup that fails where you can see it.

choices.text: Drawing the course from a saved copy of the object
choices.why: That draws something that no longer exists as if it were current.

choices.text: Ignoring the saved state and every future one
choices.why: One stale id does not make saving wrong.

prompt: Android's guide says to store in saved state a minimal amount of data, such as an ___.
A team saves the whole open course, with its sessions, in rememberSaveable. It works for every tester. Which user meets the crash first?

choices.text: The newest user, with an empty plan
choices.why: An empty plan saves a tiny state.

choices.text: The most active user, whose plan is largest
choices.why: Right. The saved state grows with the plan until it passes the Binder limit.

choices.text: Any user who rotates the phone while the form is open
choices.why: Rotation saves the same state the testers saved; the size is what differs.

choices.text: An iPhone user
choices.why: rememberSaveable is Android's.

prompt: Which belong in the planner's saved UI state? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the open course's id
choices.why: Yes: what was selected, as an id.

choices.text: the scroll position
choices.why: Yes: where the user was.

choices.text: the half-typed minutes, as a string
choices.why: Yes: what they had started.

choices.text: the list of all sessions
choices.why: That is data, and it lives in the database.

choices.text: the week's total
choices.why: It is derived; recompute it.
